lesson_title: A Tadpole Meets a Grain of Sand: The Two Gametes Compared
hook_text: The biggest cell in your body is just visible to your eye. The smallest one decides if you are a boy or a girl.
clip_script: Meet the two travellers. The sperm is a tiny tadpole, a twentieth of a millimetre long. Its head holds 23 chromosomes and wears a cap of digging enzymes to get through the egg's coat. Its neck is stuffed with mitochondria, power stations for the swim. Its tail whips it forward. No packed lunch, built light and fast, and made in the testes at more than a hundred million a day. The egg is the biggest cell in your body, a tenth of a millimetre, like a grain of fine sand. It also holds 23 chromosomes, plus a food store for the first days of life, wrapped in a jelly coat that slams shut once one sperm gets in. It cannot move: tiny waving hairs in the oviduct carry it along. Now the twist. Every egg carries an X chromosome. Each sperm carries an X or a Y. X plus X, a girl. Y plus X, a boy. So the sperm, from the father, decides. Half each, but Dad's half picks the sex.
visual_style: A sperm and an egg drawn to scale side by side, then zoomed; labels pop on head, middle piece and tail; cilia ripple to carry the egg; X and Y letters snap onto an X to show XX and XY.
pacing: Quick tour of the sperm, a slower beat on the giant egg, a sharp reveal on X and Y.
call_to_action: Watch the full lesson and label the sperm's head, middle piece and tail with their jobs.
